text: The Winnipeg Falcons were a senior men's amateur ice hockey team based in Winnipeg, Manitoba. The team won the 1920 Allan Cup as part of the Manitoba Hockey League, where they defeated the Selkirk Fishermen 5–3 to claim the championship, and this victory earned them the right to represent Canada at the 1920 Summer Olympics in Antwerp, Belgium. There, the Falcons won Canada's first Olympic gold medal in ice hockey by outscoring their opponents 29–1 over three games. The team was founded in 1911, primarily composed of Icelandic Canadian players who faced ethnic prejudice and were excluded from other Winnipeg teams; their roots trace back to the Icelandic Athletic Club formed in 1898, which merged in 1908 into a single team. In their first season, 1911–1912, they finished last in their league, but after Konnie Johannesson and Frank Fredrickson joined in 1912, they became league champions. During the First World War, seven of the eight players enlisted and went overseas; two, Frank Thorsteinson and George Cumbers, died in the war, and the remaining five returned in 1919 to reassemble the team. The Canadian Amateur Hockey Association (CAHA) selected the Falcons as the Allan Cup champions to represent Canada at the Olympics instead of forming a national all-star team. W. A. Hewitt, who oversaw finances and reported on the Games for Canadian newspapers, served as a father and mother figure to the team and sailed with them aboard the SS Melita from Saint John to Liverpool and then to Antwerp. Upon returning home via the SS Grampian from Le Havre to Quebec City, the Falcons were celebrated as conquering heroes, with each player receiving a gold watch from the City of Winnipeg and a private dinner held in honor of Hewitt and his wife, who were presented with a silver cup inscribed with the number 13—representing the number of people who traveled to the Olympics and the team's lucky number. The Falcons were inducted into the Manitoba Hockey Hall of Fame in the team category, and their legacy is honored in the Hockey Hall of Fame, Manitoba Sports Hall of Fame and Museum, and in a 2014 Heritage Minute segment narrated by George Stroumboulopoulos and featuring Jared Keeso. In 2004, Hockey Canada used a replica yellow and black jersey of the Falcons as alternate uniforms during the World Cup of Hockey against Team USA, and later that year, the national junior team wore replicas of the Falcons' gold and black uniforms in a pre-tournament game in Winnipeg. On July 31, 2019, Parks Canada designated the Falcons' 1920 Olympic victory as a "National Historical Event." The Icelandic national hockey team features the Icelandic Falcon and the Canadian maple leaf on their jerseys in honor of the Falcons. Five other players—Harvey Benson, Ed Stephenson, Connie Neil, Babs Dunlop, and Sam Laxdal—contributed to the 1919–20 season but were not part of the Olympic roster. The first member to pass away was Chris Fridfinnson, who died in 1938 at age 40; the last surviving member was Mike Goodman, who died in 1991 at age 93.
